title: Open Call: Vector-Borne Diseases Research Grant Programme (Nepal) - fundsforNGOs
description: Open Call: Vector-Borne Diseases Research Grant Programme (Nepal)  fundsforNGOs
publisher.title: fundsforNGOs
full_article:
The Vector Borne Disease Research and Training Centre (VBDRTC) is inviting Master’s and PhD students in Nepal to apply for research grants supporting innovative studies on vector-borne diseases and public health priorities. The programme supports operational and implementation research in areas such as malaria, dengue, kala-azar, lymphatic filariasis, scrub typhus and Japanese encephalitis, with emphasis on climate resilience, surveillance, vector control and evidence-based health policy.

What Is the Vector-Borne Disease Research Grant Programme?

The research grant programme is organized by the Vector Borne Disease Research and Training Centre (VBDRTC) under Nepal’s Ministry of Health and Population.

The programme aims to strengthen Nepal’s capacity to generate scientific evidence for the prevention, control and elimination of vector-borne diseases.

It particularly encourages research that responds to emerging public health challenges, including:

Climate change.

Ecological and environmental changes.

Imported infections.

Changing disease transmission patterns.

Vector resistance.

Health inequalities.

Gaps in surveillance and outbreak preparedness.

The programme also promotes multidisciplinary research and One Health approaches, linking human health with environmental and ecological factors.

Why Is Vector-Borne Disease Research Important in Nepal?

Vector-borne diseases remain an important public health concern in Nepal.

Changes in climate, ecosystems, human mobility and disease transmission patterns can affect where and when vector-borne diseases occur.

Research can help public health authorities improve:

Disease surveillance.

Early outbreak detection.

Vector control.

Diagnostic systems.

Community engagement.

Climate-resilient health planning.

Border health measures.

Disease elimination strategies.

Evidence-based policymaking.

The grant programme therefore aims to support research that can generate practical evidence for Nepal’s health system.

What Research Areas Are Supported?

Applicants can propose research within the programme’s priority themes.

Key research areas include:

Disease surveillance systems

Medical and public health entomology

Climate and health

Disease elimination

Vector control

Diagnostic methods

Community engagement

Digital epidemiology

Border health

Outbreak preparedness and response

Health equity

Public health innovation

Vector and drug resistance monitoring

Implementation science

Operational research

Implementation research

Proposals should demonstrate a clear connection to vector-borne disease prevention, control, elimination or related public health priorities in Nepal.

Which Diseases Can Be Studied?

The programme has a particular focus on important vector-borne and related diseases in Nepal, including:

Malaria.

Dengue.

Kala-azar.

Lymphatic filariasis.

Scrub typhus.

Japanese encephalitis.

Research proposals may examine epidemiology, transmission, surveillance, diagnostics, prevention, treatment implementation, vector behaviour, community practices or other relevant aspects, provided they align with the programme’s research priorities.

Who Is Eligible?

The grant is specifically intended for students undertaking postgraduate research in Nepal.

Applicants must:

Be enrolled in a Master’s or PhD programme .

. Be enrolled at a recognized university or academic institution in Nepal .

. Be a Nepali national .

. Propose research relevant to the programme’s priority themes.

Ensure the research complies with applicable national ethical requirements.

The grant can be used to support research that forms part of the applicant’s Master’s dissertation or PhD thesis.

Principal Investigator Requirement

Each research project must have one Principal Investigator (PI).

An individual Principal Investigator cannot submit more than one proposal under the programme.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposal clearly identifies the responsible Principal Investigator and avoids duplicate submissions.

Research Ethics Requirements

Proposed research must comply with the National Ethical Guideline for Health Research of the Nepal Health Research Council (NHRC).

Applicants should consider ethical requirements during proposal development, particularly when research involves:

Human participants.

Patient information.

Community-level data.

Biological samples.

Sensitive health information.

Field-based epidemiological research.

Where required, applicants should ensure that appropriate ethical approval processes are followed.

What Should a Strong Research Proposal Include?

A strong proposal should clearly explain the public health problem and how the proposed research will contribute to addressing it.

The research proposal should establish:

The research problem.

The background and rationale.

Research objectives.

Research questions or hypotheses where applicable.

Proposed methodology.

Study population or research setting.

Data collection and analysis methods.

Expected results.

Potential public health significance.

Relevance to Nepal’s vector-borne disease priorities.

Ethical considerations.

Applicants should demonstrate that the proposed study is scientifically sound, feasible and relevant to public health needs in Nepal.

How to Apply for the Research Grant

Applications must be submitted electronically.

Step 1: Confirm Eligibility

Before preparing the application, confirm that you:

Are a Nepali national.

Are enrolled in a Master’s or PhD programme.

Study at a recognized institution in Nepal.

Have a research topic aligned with the programme priorities.

Step 2: Select a Research Topic

Choose a clearly defined vector-borne disease or public health issue relevant to Nepal.

The research should fit within one or more of the programme’s priority areas, such as surveillance, entomology, climate-health, vector control, diagnostics or implementation science.

Step 3: Develop the Research Proposal

Prepare a scientifically rigorous proposal explaining the problem, objectives, methodology and expected contribution.

If the grant will support your thesis or dissertation, clearly explain how the proposed research fits within your academic programme.

Step 4: Prepare Supporting Documents

The application should include:

Research proposal.

Curriculum vitae (CV).

Copy of citizenship certificate.

Recommendation letter from the supervisor or department head.

Applicants should ensure that all documents are complete and presented in the required format.

Step 5: Submit the Application

Applications must be:

Submitted electronically.

Written in English .

. Provided in PDF format .

. Sent to vbdrtc.mohp@gmail.com.

Applicants should carefully check the submitted PDF and supporting documents before sending the application.

Step 6: Participate in Proposal Presentation if Selected

Following initial screening and evaluation, selected applicants may be invited to present their research proposal virtually.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to explain their research question, methodology, expected outcomes and public health relevance clearly.

How Are Proposals Evaluated?

Applications undergo eligibility screening followed by research evaluation.

Proposals are assessed on factors including:

Relevance: Alignment with Nepal’s vector-borne disease and public health priorities.

Alignment with Nepal’s vector-borne disease and public health priorities. Scientific merit: Strength and quality of the research concept.

Strength and quality of the research concept. Significance: Potential contribution to public health knowledge or practice.

Potential contribution to public health knowledge or practice. Methodological quality: Appropriateness and feasibility of the proposed methods.

Appropriateness and feasibility of the proposed methods. Overall quality: Coherence, clarity and completeness of the proposal.

A proposal should therefore demonstrate both scientific quality and practical relevance.

Alignment With Nepal’s Health Priorities

The programme supports national and international health priorities, including:

National Health Policy 2019

Nepal Health Sector Strategic Plan

National Malaria Strategic Plan 2025–2030

Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)

Research that addresses climate-related health risks, disease elimination, surveillance capacity and evidence-informed policymaking can contribute to these broader priorities.

Why This Research Grant Matters

The programme provides postgraduate researchers with an opportunity to contribute directly to Nepal’s evidence base on vector-borne diseases.

Supported research can help strengthen:

Local research capacity.

Disease surveillance.

Climate-resilient public health systems.

Vector control strategies.

Community-based interventions.

Disease elimination efforts.

Evidence-informed health policies.

One Health research approaches.

For Master’s and PhD students, the grant can also provide an opportunity to connect academic research with real-world public health challenges.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Applicants should carefully avoid:

Applying without meeting the Nepali nationality requirement.

Submitting a proposal unrelated to the programme’s research themes.

Failing to demonstrate relevance to Nepal.

Submitting more than one proposal as the same Principal Investigator.

Providing an unclear or poorly justified methodology.

Ignoring ethical requirements.

Omitting the supervisor or department head recommendation letter.

Forgetting to include the citizenship document.

Submitting the application in a format other than the required PDF.

Writing the proposal without explaining its potential public health impact.

Tips for a Strong Application

Applicants can strengthen their proposals by:

Clearly defining a specific research problem.

Using current evidence to establish the research gap.

Connecting the study to Nepal’s public health priorities.

Choosing realistic and achievable research objectives.

Providing a detailed methodology.

Explaining how findings could be applied.

Addressing climate change or other emerging drivers where relevant.

Demonstrating ethical and community considerations.

Keeping the proposal focused and easy to evaluate.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who can apply for the VBDRTC research grant?

The programme is open to Nepali nationals enrolled in Master’s or PhD programmes at recognized universities or academic institutions in Nepal.

Can the grant support a Master’s thesis or PhD dissertation?

Yes. The grant may be used as part of a student’s Master’s dissertation or PhD thesis, provided the research meets the programme’s requirements.

What diseases can applicants research?

Priority diseases include malaria, dengue, kala-azar, lymphatic filariasis, scrub typhus and Japanese encephalitis, along with related vector-borne disease and public health research areas.

What research themes are supported?

Priority themes include surveillance, entomology, climate-health, disease elimination, vector control, diagnostics, community engagement, digital epidemiology, border health, outbreak preparedness, health equity, innovation, resistance monitoring and implementation science.

Can one Principal Investigator submit multiple proposals?

No. Each project must have one Principal Investigator, and a Principal Investigator cannot apply for more than one proposal.

What documents must applicants submit?

Applicants must submit the research proposal, CV, copy of citizenship certificate and a recommendation letter from their supervisor or department head.

How should applications be submitted?

Applications must be submitted electronically in English as a PDF to vbdrtc.mohp@gmail.com. Applicants should ensure that all required documents are included before submission.

Conclusion

The VBDRTC Research Grant Programme provides Master’s and PhD students in Nepal with an opportunity to conduct relevant research on vector-borne diseases, climate-related health risks, surveillance, disease elimination and public health innovation. Applicants should develop focused, scientifically rigorous proposals that address Nepal’s health priorities, comply with national research ethics requirements and clearly demonstrate how their findings can strengthen disease prevention, control and evidence-based health policy.

title: Nepal could be tomorrow’s Afghanistan, or maybe New Zealand: ICC Chief Executive Sanjog Gupta - Sportstar
description: Nepal could be tomorrow’s Afghanistan, or maybe New Zealand: ICC Chief Executive Sanjog Gupta  Sportstar
publisher.title: Sportstar
full_article:
Nepal represents enormous potential for cricket and could be tomorrow’s Afghanistan or even New Zealand, ICC Chief Executive Sanjog Gupta said.

The ICC has pumped nearly $5 million into Nepal’s cricket development in the last two years and has awarded the country co-hosting rights for next year’s Under-19 Women’s World Cup.

Sanjog told Reuters that the Land of Himalayas has massive potential in the sport: “Not because the country is a significant commercial market, but because of their rapidly improving standards ⁠of performance and the scale of fandom the sport enjoys in the country.”

He opined that Nepal belonged to the global stage and could be the association nation to watch out for in the coming years.

“They could be tomorrow’s Afghanistan, or tomorrow’s ​New Zealand for that matter,” Sanjog said.

“They have developed an elite player ⁠pool which is consistently breaking through the ICC pathways and not only featuring at our marquee events, but proving that they belong on the global stage.”

The ICC official felt Nepal benefitted from a deep passionate fanbase. “Fans today are also the players of tomorrow”.

“One of my personal highlights from the T20 World Cup 2026 was the sea of red at the Wankhede (Stadium), which had turned up to support Nepal against Scotland,” Sanjog said.

Nepal beat Scotland by seven wickets to claim its first victory on that world stage since 2014, although ‌both teams had already been eliminated.

(Inputs from Reuters)

title: Nepal PM Told To Ditch Sunglasses In Parliament, Gets Medical Exemption - NDTV
description: Nepal PM Told To Ditch Sunglasses In Parliament, Gets Medical Exemption  NDTV
publisher.title: NDTV
full_article:
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah may keep his signature dark sunglasses on in the legislature due to medical reasons, an official said Tuesday, after the parliament speaker had advised against it.

The rapper-turned-politician better known as "Balen" has rarely been seen in public without his trademark rectangular shades.

The 36-year-old premier has been seen wearing them everywhere from campaign rallies to official engagements and even in his formal portrait after taking office in March.

Earlier this month, Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal advised against wearing dark glasses in the chamber, citing criticism by the public that such eyewear is out of place in the national legislature.

But Shah appears to have won an exemption.

"A report has been submitted to the secretariat pointing to medical reasons for the respected prime minister to need sunglasses," the parliament secretariat's deputy spokesman Ananta Prasad Koirala told AFP.

Koirala said Shah would be allowed to wear the glasses in parliament if they were medically necessary in bright light.

Shah, who has kept a low profile since taking office, is expected to appear for a parliament session on Wednesday.

The dark glasses, often paired with an all-black outfit, have become a defining feature of Shah's public persona since his successful campaign to become the mayor of Kathmandu in 2022.

title: From Business and Media to Inner Growth and Social Impact: Master Jiumei Brings InLight to Nepal - Yahoo Finance
description: From Business and Media to Inner Growth and Social Impact: Master Jiumei Brings InLight to Nepal  Yahoo Finance
publisher.title: Yahoo Finance
full_article:
Today, InLight has developed into an influential Asian American-founded organization focused on inner development, spiritual education and public service. Its work has received recognition and commendations from government authorities in California and the City of San Francisco.

InLight's publicly listed programs include meditation, mindfulness, yoga,breathwork, dynamic meditation, silent retreats, deep introspection, fasting retreats, extended periods of darkness retreat, leadership training, youth programs, and practices involving tea and incense. The organization also conducts meditation programs, spiritual journeys, retreats and charitable initiatives across multiple U.S. states and internationally.

Jiumei has also appeared at professional and educational forums in the United States and has been invited to speak at leading universities, including Harvard, Stanford,Yale, Princeton, MIT, Columbia, UC Berkeley, USC and California Institute of Technology, where she has explored questions surrounding human development and inner growth.A number of research and collaborative initiatives are also reportedly underway.

In May 2025, Jiumei was invited to speak at TEDxCSTU, an event organized in Silicon Valley with a focus on the relationship between human intelligence and human development.

Technology and human development have since become important themes in her work. Her educational philosophy emphasizes meditation, self-awareness and emotional balance as practical tools that can be integrated into modern everyday life.

In June 2025, Jiumei was invited to participate in a TED event of international reach, where she reflected on the lessons she drew from two life-and-death experiences. She presented the idea that "peace is the best state of life," offering a perspective on human fulfillment that moves beyond an achievement-centered definition of success and instead emphasizes inner growth, selfawakening and, ultimately, the transformation of inner development into service to others.

From Inner Growth to Social Action

In Nepal, InLight has extended its focus on inner development into a more tangible sphere of social engagement.

In July, Jiumei led nearly 20 core members of the InLight international community from the United States, China, Canada and other countries to Arya Tara School, founded in 2000 by Ani Choying Drolma.

The delegation engaged with Choying Drolma, teachers and students through discussions and cultural activities, including conversations on women's issues and Buddhist chanting. Members of the InLight delegation learned about the history and mission of the school and visited its community classrooms.

The experience deeply affected the group. For the InLight delegation, the visit underscored a central principle: inner awakening cannot be limited to achieving personal peace. The circumstances in which women live are an important measure of social wellbeing.When poverty, family circumstances or other hardships deprive women of meaningful choices and opportunities, genuine social well-being remains incomplete.

For InLight, compassion therefore needs to move beyond an internal state of mind and become practical support for vulnerable women and children. In this sense, the visit represented a concrete expression of the organization's broader philosophy of creating a better world from the inside out.

Members of the InLight delegation also contributed approximately 700,000 Nepalese rupees to support the school's educational and charitable activities.

The visit brought together two women whose backgrounds could hardly be more different, yet whose life journeys have increasingly converged around questions of human development, compassion and service.

Ani Choying Drolma and Her Work in Nepal

Ani Choying Drolma entered monastic life in Nepal at the age of 13 and later achieved international recognition for her Buddhist chanting and musical work.

Her artistic career eventually became a platform for social engagement,particularly in education and healthcare.

Arya Tara School is one of her principal educational initiatives. The school combines modern academic education with Buddhist studies and provides educational opportunities for children of single mothers as well as young Buddhist nuns.

In 2010, Choying Drolma also founded the Aarogya Foundation, which focuses on kidney healthcare, including dialysis and other forms of renal treatment.

On August 16, Master Jiumei and members of the InLight team visited a dialysis center supported by the Aarogya Foundation at Chhetrapati Community Hospital in Kathmandu.

During the visit, Jiumei spoke with medical staff about the operation of the dialysis center and the circumstances of patients receiving treatment. She also personally visited patients at their bedsides, listened attentively to their experiences with illness and treatment, held their hands and offered words of encouragement and support.

Jiumei and the InLight team also made financial and clothing donations to support the patients and the medical center.

Following the visit, Jiumei and Choying Drolma held in-depth discussions on Nepal's public healthcare system, women's health and ways of supporting vulnerable communities.

InLight's Broader Engagement in Nepal

The August visits were part of InLight's broader engagement with Nepal.

According to InLight, the organization and its supporters have provided financial assistance to a range of educational and charitable initiatives in Nepal, including Lumbini Buddhist University, the Lumbini World Peace Pagoda,Arya Tara School, monastic schools,preschools serving children from disadvantaged communities, Buddhist Sangha communities and programs supporting children in impoverished mountainous areas.

InLight estimates that the cumulative value of this support has exceeded 48 million Nepalese rupees. The figure represents an accumulated level of support provided over an extended period to various charitable and educational initiatives in Nepal.

For Jiumei, however, the significance of coming to Nepal extends beyond charitable giving.

As the birthplace of the Buddha,Nepal offers a unique setting for exploring the relationship between inner balance, compassion, Buddhist wisdom and human development.

Jiumei has brought entrepreneurs, financial professionals, scientists, technology specialists, educators and artists from different countries to Nepal, encouraging them to experience the country's social environment, cultural heritage, Buddhist traditions and distinctive approach to well-being, while reflecting on broader questions concerning modern life and human flourishing.

From Inner Fulfillment to Social Impact

Jiumei and Ani Choying Drolma represent two very different paths through life.

Jiumei emerged from the worlds of business, fashion and media before turning toward meditation, inner development and spiritual education. Choying Drolma emerged from the Himalayan Buddhist tradition and transformed an internationally recognized artistic career into a platform for education, healthcare and humanitarian service.

One moved from professional success toward inner exploration and ultimately toward service to human well-being. The other moved from monastic practice toward a life of social engagement and philanthropy.

Their meeting in Nepal brings these two trajectories together around a practical question:

How can inner growth make a lasting and meaningful contribution to the well-being of others?

For Jiumei, meditation and personal development are not intended to separate people from society. Rather, they are meant to help individuals become more aware,balanced and responsible participants in the world, while cultivating what she regards as the highest qualities of human compassion and wisdom.

Nepal has given this philosophy a concrete social dimension: education, healthcare, care for vulnerable communities, responses to present-day challenges and long-term investment in human development. In this framework, compassion and wisdom are not merely ideals; they can be translated into measurable,practical action.

As artificial intelligence and other technologies rapidly reshape society and everyday life, Jiumei argues that technological and scientific progress must be accompanied by greater attention to human well-being and the development of the inner life.

That perspective is reflected in the arc of her own journey - from China's business and media industries, to a new chapter of inner development in the United States, and now to humanitarian engagement and service in Nepal and beyond.

Her work reflects a broader proposition: the future of human development may depend not only on how rapidly technology advances,but also on how deeply humanity learns to understand itself.

About InLight Foundation

InLight Foundation is a formally registered non-profit organization in the United States, founded by Teacher Jiumei and currently operated entirely by volunteers. Its aim is to help more modern urban dwellers experience the charm of meditation, improve their quality of life, and gain joy of mind and body.

With the continuous integration of digital payments, Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence technologies into the retail industry, automation and digitalization have become important trends in the global retail market. BV Nepal, focusing on smart vending equipment and digital retail solutions, is gradually transforming from a single smart vending equipment provider into a comprehensive smart retail ecosystem.

BV Nepal began exploring the smart vending and automated retail sector in 2022. During its early development stage, the company focused on smart vending equipment and operational models, aiming to reduce dependence on traditional retail labor while improving consumer shopping convenience.









In 2023, BV Nepal further optimized its equipment and software systems. The company expanded its smart vending solutions into payment systems, inventory management, sales data analysis, and remote operation capabilities, while exploring applications in offices, commercial spaces, campuses, communities, hotels, hospitals, and transportation hubs.

Since 2024, BV Nepal has strengthened the integration of equipment, software, data, and supply chain systems. Smart vending machines have gradually evolved into intelligent retail terminals connecting consumers, products, payments, and operational management.

In 2025, StarBox Vending Creative Marketing Pty Ltd was officially registered in Australia, establishing an important foundation for BV Nepal's global development strategy.

Since 2026, BV Nepal has continued expanding overseas markets and extending its business scope from traditional vending categories to broader smart retail applications including general merchandise, electronics, medical products, and personal care products.

Looking ahead, BV Nepal plans to build a smart retail network based on intelligent hardware, artificial intelligence, IoT, cloud data, and supply chain systems, while exploring localized operational models according to the characteristics of different markets.

title: Fall Season Starts On Manaslu - Explorersweb »

full_article:
The fall season in Nepal has begun, and Manaslu is the most popular ascent.

The Expedition Operators’ Association of Nepal (EOA) has formed a team of Sherpa climbers to fix the ropes. The seven-member team, led by Chhiring Bhote, will depart to the base of the mountain tomorrow. Lopsang Bhote, Ngima Sherpa, Pam Dorjee Sherpa, Furi Sherpa, Pasang Gyaljen Sherpa, and Karma Sarki Sherpa will fix the ropes to the summit and plant a Nepal flag on top.

Meanwhile, commercial expedition companies are rushing to set up the huge base camp and will soon start building Camp 1 on a large snowy plain.

Some images of staff setting up Base Camp on Manaslu. Photo: Satori Adventures

An essential task

These days, professional Sherpa teams fix the normal routes on Nepal’s 8,000’ers from bottom to top, and then everyone else on the mountain follows. Therefore, the rope-fixing work marks progress on the mountains. There are rare exceptions, odd teams of self-sufficient climbers who climb in off-season. On Manaslu, all commercial expeditions climb in September and October.

Alex Moroz of Ukraine and Mark Ablovacky of Russia climbed Manaslu in spring this year, and had the mountain all to themselves. This marked a rare alpine approach with no supplementary oxygen or support.

Climbers go up fixed ropes on Manaslu in 2022. Photo: World Sherpas/Furtemba Sherpa

With modern commercial methods, expedition duration is cut in half. Last year, the rope-fixers achieved the first summits of the season on September 21. By October 2, the mountain had closed with over 600 summits. That left enough time for local guides and support staff, as well as some climbers, to move to other mountains.

Slightly fewer permits expected

According to data from Nepal’s Department of Tourism (DoT), the final summit tally for Manaslu in 2025 was 659, including both foreigners and locals. It is worth noting that some Sherpa guides reached the summit more than once. For the upcoming season, sources at the DoT estimate they will grant around 300 permits to international climbers. If their estimate is reasonably accurate, that means a decrease from 2025, when they granted 381 permits.

The huge 2024 Manaslu Base Camp. Photo: Seven Summit Treks

Things may change in the next few weeks. Manaslu could attract some of the climbers who had planned to climb Cho Oyu or Shisha Pangma, after the China-Tibet Mountaineering Association confirmed they will ban foreign expeditions on the two Tibetan 8,000’ers.

Pakistan vs. Nepal

There might also be some last-minute additions from climbers who attempted 8,000’ers in Pakistan. The Pakistan summer season has seen few summits because of bad weather. The season ended abruptly when an avalanche killed ten climbers on Broad Peak on July 30. It is the first time since the COVID pandemic in 2020 that no one has summited K2. The few teams on the mountain aborted their summit push after the terrible news from neighboring Broad Peak.

Lukas Supergan of Poland was one of the first climbers to announce their plans for Manaslu. He will attempt the mountain without using supplemental oxygen or Sherpa support.

Supergan had been pondering whether to climb in Nepal or Pakistan this year. In 2025, he was the last climber to retreat from Broad Peak because of bad conditions on the route. This year, he feared finding the same problems on Broad Peak and eventually chose to climb Manaslu in September. “The events of this summer showed that giving up on Pakistan was the right decision,” Supergan wrote on social media.

यूक्रेन केरऽ एलेक्स मोरोज आरू रूस केरऽ मार्क अब्लोवाकी न॑ ई साल बसंत म॑ मनास्लू प॑ चढ़ी गेलऽ छेलै, आरू ई पहाड़ सब कुछ खुद लेली छेलै । ई एकटा दुर्लभ अल्पाइन दृष्टिकोण के चिन्हित करलकै जेकरा म॑ कोनो पूरक ऑक्सीजन या समर्थन नै छेलै ।

कनि कम परमिट के उम्मीद अछि

नेपाल के पर्यटन विभाग के आंकड़ा के अनुसार 2025 में मनसलू के लेल अंतिम शिखर सम्मेलन 659 छल, जाहि में विदेशी आ स्थानीय दुनु शामिल छल. ध्यान देबय योग्य बात ई जे किछु शेर्पा गाइड एक सं बेसी बेर शिखर पर पहुंचल छलाह. आबै वाला सीजन लेली डॉट केरऽ सूत्रऽ के अनुमान छै कि वू अंतरराष्ट्रीय पर्वतारोही सिनी क॑ लगभग ३०० परमिट देतै । अगर हुनकऽ अनुमान यथोचित रूप स॑ सही छै त॑ एकरऽ मतलब छै कि २०२५ स॑ कमी, जब॑ हुनी ३८१ परमिट देल॑ छेलै ।

विशाल 2024 के मनसलू बेस कैंप। फोटो : सात शिखर पदयात्रा

अगिला किछु सप्ताह मे हालात बदलि सकैत अछि। चीन-तिब्बत पर्वतारोहण संघ केरऽ पुष्टि के बाद कि हुनी दूनू तिब्बती 8,000’ers प॑ विदेशी अभियान प॑ रोक लगाबै वाला कुछ पर्वतारोही क॑ मनसलू आकर्षित करी सकै छै ।

पाकिस्तान बनाम नेपाल

पाकिस्तान में 8000’ers के प्रयास करय वाला पर्वतारोही के अंतिम समय में किछ जोड़ सेहो भ सकैत अछि. पाकिस्तान के गर्मी के मौसम में खराब मौसम के कारण शिखर सम्मेलन कम देखल गेल अछि. मौसम अचानक समाप्त भ गेल जखन 30 जुलाई कए ब्रॉड पीक पर हिमस्खलन मे दसटा पर्वतारोही क मौत भ गेल।2020 मे कोविड महामारी क बाद इ पहिल बेर अछि जे के2 क शिखर पर कियो नहि पहुंचल अछि। पहाड़ पर किछु टीम पड़ोसी ब्रॉड पीक सं आयल भयानक खबर के बाद अपन शिखर धक्का के गर्भपात क देलक.

पोलैंड केरऽ लुकास सुपरगन मनसलू लेली अपनऽ योजना के घोषणा करै वाला पहिलऽ पर्वतारोही म॑ स॑ एक छेलै । ओ बिना पूरक ऑक्सीजन या शेर्पा सपोर्ट के प्रयोग केने पहाड़ के प्रयास करताह।

सुपरगन एहि साल नेपाल मे चढ़ब आकि पाकिस्तान मे चढ़ब ताहि पर चिंतन क रहल छल। 2025 मे ओ अंतिम पर्वतारोही छलाह जे ब्रॉड पीक सं पाछू हटि गेलाह, कारण एहि रूट पर खराब हालत छल. एहि साल हुनका ब्रॉड पीक पर सेहो एहने समस्या भेटबाक आशंका छलनि आ अंततः सितंबर मे मनसलू पर चढ़ब पसिन केलनि। सुपरगन न॑ सोशल मीडिया प॑ लिखलकै कि ई गर्मी केरऽ घटना स॑ पता चललै कि पाकिस्तान स॑ हार मानना ​​सही फैसला छेलै ।

title: Supporting Community Health from New Haven to Nepal - UConn Today
description: Supporting Community Health from New Haven to Nepal  UConn Today
publisher.title: UConn Today
full_article:
Asked about the driving force for his lab’s work, associate professor Roman Shrestha says it all comes down to “really making a difference for the vulnerable populations we work with.”

The Shrestha Lab is a group of interdisciplinary researchers dedicated to improving health outcomes and quality of life for people across the globe, especially those who face barriers to accessing the traditional healthcare system. They focus on developing solutions that can easily plug into existing needs, including innovative new service programs and digital health initiatives like apps and wearable devices.

The lab has a strong international focus, with specific projects focused on supporting mental health, substance use, and HIV prevention among sexual minority populations in Malaysia and Nepal. But they also work with communities closer to home.

Researchers at the Shrestha Lab have a longtime partnership with the New Haven Syringe Services Program, hosted by the Yale Community Healthcare Van in New Haven. Through this partnership, they work to support the mental and physical health of people who inject drugs (PWID) here in Connecticut, while also laying the groundwork for interventions that can be adopted anywhere.

Suicide Prevention with SAFE-SSP

One of these interventions, Suicide Assessment and Facilitated Engagement in Syringe Services Programs (SAFE-SSP), recently received seed funding from the UConn Institute for Collaboration on Health, Intervention, and Policy ( InCHIP ) and UConn Health Disparities Institute ( HDI ).

It aims to understand how mental health and suicide prevention efforts can be better integrated into existing harm reduction services.

“Syringe services programs and other community-based harm reduction programs are very trusted, low-barrier spaces that reach people who may not regularly use the traditional healthcare system,” says Shrestha Lab manager and assistant research professor Kamal Gautam. This makes them ideal sites for health outreach efforts.

Assistant research professor Kamal Gautam presents on the SAFE-SSP program at the UConn InCHIP Research Forum. (Courtesy of Roman Shrestha)

These programs excel at treating physical health – they provide clean needles, and they also often provide wound care and medication to treat opioid use disorder like suboxone. But they may not always have the resources to support complex mental health needs, according to Gautam.

As a result, many participants’ significant mental health needs are going unmet. According to the lab’s recently published study among New Haven syringe services program participants, over one-third reported suicidal ideation within the past two weeks, and nearly 85% reported experiencing at least one barrier to accessing mental health services.

Recognizing this need, Shrestha Lab researchers are working to develop a suicide screening tool and referral pathway that could be used in harm reduction settings.

Most existing tools were created for very different contexts – usually in emergency care settings, where they can only be used by physicians or psychiatrists. That doesn’t match the reality of syringe services program participants, who are more likely to engage with healthcare providers and staff at the syringe services programs.

The researchers realized that this group needed a unique screening tool which would meet the needs of both patients and providers. Its use should be as seamless as possible and allow the participants to either receive mental health care onsite or receive a warm hand-off to appropriate services.

“Throughout this project, what we want to learn is how suicide risk can be discussed without increasing stigma or discouraging service use,” Gautam says.

Shrestha Lab members at the Society of Behavioral Medicine 2025 Conference. (Courtesy of Roman Shrestha)

He explains that the team is particularly interested in making sure the screening tool is something that benefits both the clients and staff.

“[Health researchers] always try to think from the patients’ perspective, but we sometimes miss the people who are actually delivering the intervention – the staff or the healthcare providers,” Gautam says. “With this project, we wanted to make sure we were exploring that piece – are they [the providers] comfortable delivering the intervention? Do they have what they need? And at the same time, we don’t want to overburden them.”

At the conclusion of this pilot project, the team will have the “preliminary evidence needed to develop and test more comprehensive suicide prevention intervention across syringe services programs and other community-based harm reduction settings,” says Gautam.

Nurse Practitioner–Led PrEP

Another recent initiative from the Shrestha Lab is a publication in the Journal of the Association of Nurses in AIDS Care (JANAC) , first-authored by Gautam.

The article is based on findings from another pilot project in New Haven, focused on decreasing barriers to accessing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). PrEP is an umbrella term for medications that are incredibly effective at preventing HIV – providing up to 99% HIV protection from sex and up to 74% effective HIV protection from injection drug use, when taken as prescribed.

Still, as with mental health care, it can be challenging for people who inject drugs to access these treatments. Time, money, and logistics all pose hurdles.

For people who use substances, the care can be so fragmented.

“Typically, while trying to get on PrEP, you have to go to a clinic, be seen by a doctor, and then the doctor will have to evaluate your labs before they can prescribe the medication,” says Shrestha. “This is a huge issue for people who inject drugs, because they have different socioeconomic conditions that will prevent them from getting back to the clinic – whether it’s transportation, unstable housing, or even lack of a cell phone to get appointment and pickup reminders.”

Through a pilot program called iRaPID (Integrated Rapid Access to HIV Prevention for People Who Inject Drugs) , the researchers launched a new approach to PrEP prescription. This method eliminated the barrier of visiting a separate HIV clinic and waiting to receive a prescription – instead, nurse practitioners at the syringe services program could prescribe PrEP on the very first visit.

“For people who use substances, the care can be so fragmented,” says Shrestha. “If you want to get HIV prevention or treatment services, you go to one place; if you need medication to treat addiction, you have to go to another place.”

Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), the iRaPID program sought to instead create more of a “one-stop shop,” using the touchpoint of syringe services.

The researchers found that this type of nurse practitioner–led, same-day model was acceptable to both clinical staff and patients alike.

“We saw some very positive outcomes in terms of improving access and uptake of PrEP services within the existing harm reduction settings,” says Shrestha.

This study lays the groundwork for future, larger-scale studies to determine the feasibility of implementing this model in more contexts.

Assistant research professor Kamal Gautam (far left) and associate professor Roman Shrestha (far right) attending the International AIDS Society 2026 Conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. (Courtesy of Roman Shrestha)

Going Global

In countries across the world, Shrestha Lab researchers are working to reduce barriers to mental and physical healthcare; support harm reduction; and prevent suicide among underserved communities.

This expansive focus is why the lab’s website describes their work as sitting “at the intersection of HIV prevention and treatment, substance use, harm reduction, mental health, smoking cessation, sexual and gender minority health, and global health equity.”

It’s a complex intersection. But Gautam says that a few key principles lie at the heart of all these initiatives.

“All of our work is grounded in dignity, non-judgmentality, equity — and community partnership,” he says.

Recently funded projects within the Shrestha Lab include a new R01 award to reduce HIV-related stigma in Vietnam (a collaboration with researchers at the University of Pittsburgh) and a just-in-time adaptive intervention for suicide prevention among men who have sex with men in Nepal. Both initiatives received funding from the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Follow updates from the Shrestha Lab on their website , LinkedIn , and Instagram .

title: From Business and Media to Inner Growth and Social Impact: Master Jiumei Brings InLight to Nepal - markets.businessinsider.com
description: From Business and Media to Inner Growth and Social Impact: Master Jiumei Brings InLight to Nepal  markets.businessinsider.com
publisher.title: markets.businessinsider.com
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nepal, Aug. 25, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Master Jiumei, founder of the U.S.-based InLight International and InLight Foundation, is expanding her work in inner development and spiritual education into Nepal, seeking to connect practices of human inner growth with education, healthcare and philanthropic service.

August 2026, Jiumei led an international InLight delegation to Nepal.

The group visited Arya Tara School, founded by internationally renowned Nepali Buddhist nun and chant artist Ani Choying Drolma, as well as a dialysis center in Kathmandu supported by the Aarogya Foundation, another organization founded by Choying Drolma.

The Nepal visit represents another step in Jiumei's evolution from China's business and media world toward a broader mission centered on inner development, spiritual education and humanitarian service.

From Business and Media to Inner Growth

Jiumei,born Zhang Xiaomei, first became widely known for her achievements in China's business, fashion and media industries.

According to a 2025 profile published by The Beverly Arts, she was an entrepreneur,bestselling author and media founder who played a prominent role in China's fashion and beauty industries. The profile noted that she founded publications including China Beauty Fashion News and New Human, organized China International Beauty and Fashion Week, and authored dozens of books for women.

Her career later took a dramatically different direction, transforming her from a successful business and media figure into a prominent advocate for inner development and spiritual growth.

According to the same profile, Jiumei studied and practiced traditions including Taoism, Buddhism and ancient yoga, and traveled extensively in her search for deeper meditation and spiritual understanding. In 2016, she entered the Karme Ling Retreat Center in the United States, where she undertook an intensive retreat lasting nearly four years.

Over time, the center of gravity of her life shifted toward meditation, self-awareness and inner development. Following a profound period of personal insight and spiritual awakening, she committed herself to education and service aimed at helping others explore their own inner potential.

From Spiritual Awakening to Building InLight in the United States

In 2022, Jiumei founded InLight International.According to publicly available profiles and institutional information, the organization has expanded its programs across the United States, Canada and other countries.

In the United States, InLight has established international retreat and meditation centers in Mount Shasta and Silicon Valley, California, while developing a contemplative center in Crestone, Colorado, a location known for its spiritual and retreat communities.

Today, InLight has developed into an influential Asian American-founded organization focused on inner development, spiritual education and public service. Its work has received recognition and commendations from government authorities in California and the City of San Francisco.

InLight's publicly listed programs include meditation, mindfulness, yoga,breathwork, dynamic meditation, silent retreats, deep introspection, fasting retreats, extended periods of darkness retreat, leadership training, youth programs, and practices involving tea and incense. The organization also conducts meditation programs, spiritual journeys, retreats and charitable initiatives across multiple U.S. states and internationally.

Jiumei has also appeared at professional and educational forums in the United States and has been invited to speak at leading universities, including Harvard, Stanford,Yale, Princeton, MIT, Columbia, UC Berkeley, USC and California Institute of Technology, where she has explored questions surrounding human development and inner growth.A number of research and collaborative initiatives are also reportedly underway.

In May 2025, Jiumei was invited to speak at TEDxCSTU, an event organized in Silicon Valley with a focus on the relationship between human intelligence and human development.

Technology and human development have since become important themes in her work. Her educational philosophy emphasizes meditation, self-awareness and emotional balance as practical tools that can be integrated into modern everyday life.

In June 2025, Jiumei was invited to participate in a TED event of international reach, where she reflected on the lessons she drew from two life-and-death experiences. She presented the idea that "peace is the best state of life," offering a perspective on human fulfillment that moves beyond an achievement-centered definition of success and instead emphasizes inner growth, selfawakening and, ultimately, the transformation of inner development into service to others.

From Inner Growth to Social Action

In Nepal, InLight has extended its focus on inner development into a more tangible sphere of social engagement.

In July, Jiumei led nearly 20 core members of the InLight international community from the United States, China, Canada and other countries to Arya Tara School, founded in 2000 by Ani Choying Drolma.

The delegation engaged with Choying Drolma, teachers and students through discussions and cultural activities, including conversations on women's issues and Buddhist chanting. Members of the InLight delegation learned about the history and mission of the school and visited its community classrooms.

The experience deeply affected the group. For the InLight delegation, the visit underscored a central principle: inner awakening cannot be limited to achieving personal peace. The circumstances in which women live are an important measure of social wellbeing.When poverty, family circumstances or other hardships deprive women of meaningful choices and opportunities, genuine social well-being remains incomplete.

For InLight, compassion therefore needs to move beyond an internal state of mind and become practical support for vulnerable women and children. In this sense, the visit represented a concrete expression of the organization's broader philosophy of creating a better world from the inside out.

Members of the InLight delegation also contributed approximately 700,000 Nepalese rupees to support the school's educational and charitable activities.

The visit brought together two women whose backgrounds could hardly be more different, yet whose life journeys have increasingly converged around questions of human development, compassion and service.

Ani Choying Drolma and Her Work in Nepal

Ani Choying Drolma entered monastic life in Nepal at the age of 13 and later achieved international recognition for her Buddhist chanting and musical work.

Her artistic career eventually became a platform for social engagement,particularly in education and healthcare.

Arya Tara School is one of her principal educational initiatives. The school combines modern academic education with Buddhist studies and provides educational opportunities for children of single mothers as well as young Buddhist nuns.

In 2010, Choying Drolma also founded the Aarogya Foundation, which focuses on kidney healthcare, including dialysis and other forms of renal treatment.

On August 16, Master Jiumei and members of the InLight team visited a dialysis center supported by the Aarogya Foundation at Chhetrapati Community Hospital in Kathmandu.

During the visit, Jiumei spoke with medical staff about the operation of the dialysis center and the circumstances of patients receiving treatment. She also personally visited patients at their bedsides, listened attentively to their experiences with illness and treatment, held their hands and offered words of encouragement and support.

Jiumei and the InLight team also made financial and clothing donations to support the patients and the medical center.

Following the visit, Jiumei and Choying Drolma held in-depth discussions on Nepal's public healthcare system, women's health and ways of supporting vulnerable communities.

InLight's Broader Engagement in Nepal

The August visits were part of InLight's broader engagement with Nepal.

According to InLight, the organization and its supporters have provided financial assistance to a range of educational and charitable initiatives in Nepal, including Lumbini Buddhist University, the Lumbini World Peace Pagoda,Arya Tara School, monastic schools,preschools serving children from disadvantaged communities, Buddhist Sangha communities and programs supporting children in impoverished mountainous areas.

InLight estimates that the cumulative value of this support has exceeded 48 million Nepalese rupees. The figure represents an accumulated level of support provided over an extended period to various charitable and educational initiatives in Nepal.

For Jiumei, however, the significance of coming to Nepal extends beyond charitable giving.

As the birthplace of the Buddha,Nepal offers a unique setting for exploring the relationship between inner balance, compassion, Buddhist wisdom and human development.

Jiumei has brought entrepreneurs, financial professionals, scientists, technology specialists, educators and artists from different countries to Nepal, encouraging them to experience the country's social environment, cultural heritage, Buddhist traditions and distinctive approach to well-being, while reflecting on broader questions concerning modern life and human flourishing.

From Inner Fulfillment to Social Impact

Jiumei and Ani Choying Drolma represent two very different paths through life.

Jiumei emerged from the worlds of business, fashion and media before turning toward meditation, inner development and spiritual education. Choying Drolma emerged from the Himalayan Buddhist tradition and transformed an internationally recognized artistic career into a platform for education, healthcare and humanitarian service.

One moved from professional success toward inner exploration and ultimately toward service to human well-being. The other moved from monastic practice toward a life of social engagement and philanthropy.

Their meeting in Nepal brings these two trajectories together around a practical question:

How can inner growth make a lasting and meaningful contribution to the well-being of others?

For Jiumei, meditation and personal development are not intended to separate people from society. Rather, they are meant to help individuals become more aware,balanced and responsible participants in the world, while cultivating what she regards as the highest qualities of human compassion and wisdom.

Nepal has given this philosophy a concrete social dimension: education, healthcare, care for vulnerable communities, responses to present-day challenges and long-term investment in human development. In this framework, compassion and wisdom are not merely ideals; they can be translated into measurable,practical action.

As artificial intelligence and other technologies rapidly reshape society and everyday life, Jiumei argues that technological and scientific progress must be accompanied by greater attention to human well-being and the development of the inner life.

That perspective is reflected in the arc of her own journey - from China's business and media industries, to a new chapter of inner development in the United States, and now to humanitarian engagement and service in Nepal and beyond.

Her work reflects a broader proposition: the future of human development may depend not only on how rapidly technology advances,but also on how deeply humanity learns to understand itself.

About InLight Foundation

InLight Foundation is a formally registered non-profit organization in the United States, founded by Teacher Jiumei and currently operated entirely by volunteers. Its aim is to help more modern urban dwellers experience the charm of meditation, improve their quality of life, and gain joy of mind and body.

title: Rape and murder of 3 year old girl sparks outrage in Nepal, with protesters demanding tougher laws - CBS News
description: Rape and murder of 3 year old girl sparks outrage in Nepal, with protesters demanding tougher laws  CBS News
publisher.title: CBS News
full_article:
The rape and murder of a 3-year-old girl in Nepal has sparked widespread outrage and protests in the Himalayan country, with activists and politicians demanding tougher laws on rape, including calls for the death penalty to be imposed for the crime.

The little girl went missing from her home in Bara, about 80 miles south of the capital Kathmandu, on August 16. Her body was found at an abandoned house three days later. Police registered a case of rape and murder and have arrested nine suspects, including a bus driver and a 16-year-old boy who worked on the same bus, who they accuse of luring the girl into the attack with chocolate.

Outrage over the attack led to protests that lasted several days, with angry demonstrators, many of them young people, blocking highways around the capital.

A child and others participate in a protest in Kathmandu, Nepal, Aug. 22, 2026, demanding justice for a 3-year-old girl who was raped and murdered. Safal Prakash Shrestha/NurPhoto/Getty

Protesters shouted slogans denouncing the police and government over alleged delays in taking action to find the missing girl, and then to find the perpetrators. There has also been pointed criticism of Prime Minister Balen Shah, who came to power following Gen-Z-led protests in 2025 that led to his predecessor KP Sharma Oli being ousted.

Shah, a relatively young leader who brought hope to many in the country that systematic change in policing and other issues would be implemented, is facing criticism for failing to usher those changes — and for going on a personal tour of a picturesque mountain region in the country as the protests ramped up earlier this week.

The father of the victim alleged that police didn't respond with urgency when the family reported her missing, forcing family members to mount a search themselves.

"I raised the matter with the police," the man told The Kathmandu Post. "But they said they could not proceed merely on what I was saying, and asked me to file a formal complaint by naming suspects."

Neither the victim nor her family has been named by officials.

The protesters, along with several activists and politicians, have demanded tougher laws against rape and sexual violence.

Members of the Independent Mothers of Nepal group stage a protest in Kathmandu, Nepal, Aug. 22, 2026, demanding justice for a 3-year-old girl who was raped and killed. Safal Prakash Shrestha/NurPhoto/Getty

Government ministers met with the victim's family over the weekend and promised to review laws and create a memorial in honor of the little girl.

"Will erecting a statue bring back the life of a 3-year-old girl?" Pramila Kumari Gachhadar, a lawmaker with the opposition Nepali Congress party, asked in parliament Monday, criticizing the government's handling of the case. "An agreement paper may temporarily stop protests, and relief may ease momentary pain, but it cannot restore long-term perception of justice and trust in the state."

Another lawmaker, Prakash Pathak of the prime minister's Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), urged the government to consider the death penalty for convicted rapists, according to The Himalayan newspaper.

Nepal's constitution bars the death penalty for any crimes, so the maximum sentence a court can currently impose is life imprisonment.

"If possible, provisions for hanging rapists must be made. If not, laws should be enacted to amputate the organ used to commit the rape," added RSP lawmaker Ashika Tamang.

Nepal's Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Sobita Gautam, and Home Minister Sudan Gurung both ruled out capital punishment, however, noting that it would require amending the constitution.

Nepali law currently imposes a minimum of seven years prison for people convicted of raping an adult. In cases where the victim is under 10 years old, the possible jail term is 16 to 20 years, but it can be increased to life imprisonment depending on the circumstances of the case.

In cases of rape and murder, the punishment is life imprisonment.

An average of more than 2,500 rapes are reported in Nepal every year, including 250 in which the victims are under the age of 10, according to data compiled by the Nepal Police.

title: Nepal-US cooperation should focus on digital innovation, clean energy and trade: Minister Khanal - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal-US cooperation should focus on digital innovation, clean energy and trade: Minister Khanal  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By TRN Online, Kathmandu, Aug. 25: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has viewed that Nepal-US economic relation should be focused on three strategic sectors: digital innovation, clean energy and trade.

Addressing a function organised by the Center for Social Innovation and Foreign Policy, commemorating the 250th anniversary of American Independence, in Kathmandu today, Minister Khanal pointed at the need to expand and move forward the traditional Nepal-US relations and concentrate on investment, trade, technology and entrepreneurship.

On the occasion, Minister Khanal extended his best wishes to the Government and people of the United States on behalf of the Government and people of Nepal and highlighted the longstanding Nepal-US ties rooted in shared democratic values and constitutionalism.

With regard to digital transformation, a sector that he said the Nepal-US cooperation should focus, Minister Khanal said digital transformation should be moved forward by connecting Nepal's skilled youth and IT human resource with US innovation system and capital.

"We want to link Nepal's talented youths and IT human resource with US ecosystem of innovation and capital," he said.

As the second sector of cooperation, he mentioned expansion of cooperation on clean energy and climate resilience. Sustainable hydropower, cross border transmission line structure and Himalayan ecosystem preservation are its primary sector, he said.

title: Fact Check: Ashika Tamang’s Claim That Nepal’s Law Treats Marital Rape and Minor Rape Equally Is False - Techpana
description: Fact Check: Ashika Tamang’s Claim That Nepal’s Law Treats Marital Rape and Minor Rape Equally Is False  Techpana
publisher.title: Techpana
full_article:
Kathmandu. Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Member of Parliament Ashika Tamang has claimed that Nepal’s existing law does not classify punishment according to the nature of rape. She argued that the law treats the rape of a three-year-old girl and marital rape on the same scale and called for immediate legal reform.

However, an investigation by the TechPana FactCheck Desk has found the claim to be false. Chapter 18 of the Muluki Criminal Code of the victim. The punishment prescribed for rape of a girl below 10 years of age is substantially different from that prescribed for marital rape.

Claim

On Tuesday morning, August 25, at 8:59 am, RSP MP Ashika Tamang posted a statement on her verified Facebook page. In the post, she argued that an allegation of marital rape by a wife against her husband and the rape of a three-year-old girl cannot be treated on the same scale.

Tamang called for the law to distinguish between different forms and circumstances of rape and demanded that the process of amending the law be initiated immediately.

She wrote, “ The accusation of rape by a wife against her husband and the rape of a 3-year-old girl can never be put on the same scale. Therefore, the law should be able to differentiate the punishment according to the type of rape and the law should be amended immediately.”

By the time this fact-check was prepared, more than 14,000 people had reacted to the post. The post had also received more than 1,000 comments and 57 shares. See the post and screenshot here.

Investigation

Following Tamang’s claim that Nepal’s existing law does not classify rape according to its type and her call for immediate legal amendment, the TechPana FactCheck Desk examined the legal provisions governing rape and related offences.

The Muluki Criminal Code Act, 2074 contains provisions relating to rape under Chapter 18. The chapter deals with offences relating to force and includes provisions on related offences, punishment, compensation and limitation.

Section 219 states that no person shall commit rape. Sub-section (2) provides that sexual intercourse with a girl below 18 years of age is considered rape even if it takes place with her consent.

Sub-section (3) of Section 219 prescribes different punishments depending on the circumstances of the offence and the age of the woman or girl.

What is the punishment for rape of a woman of any age?

The law prescribes the following punishments:

Girls below 10 years of age, totally disabled women or women above 70 years of age: Life imprisonment.

Girls aged 10 to below 14 years: Imprisonment for 18 to 20 years.

Girls aged 14 to below 16 years: Imprisonment for 12 to 14 years.

Girls aged 16 to below 18 years: Imprisonment for 10 to 12 years.

Women aged 18 years or above: Imprisonment for seven to 10 years.

What is the legal system related to marital rape?

Sub-section (4) of Section 219 contains a separate provision for marital rape. If a husband forces his wife to have sexual intercourse while the marital relationship continues, he can be sentenced to imprisonment for up to five years.

However, the law does not consider the marital relationship to be continuing in cases involving legal separation from the husband, a separation proceeding, or divorce proceedings.

Sub-section (6) of Section 219 also provides for additional punishment in aggravated circumstances. These include rape committed by a person who knows they are HIV-positive or has a sexually transmitted disease, gang rape, rape of a woman who is more than six months pregnant, rape of a disabled, physically or mentally unsound woman, rape by showing a weapon, rape of a totally disabled woman and rape of a woman who has previously been sexually assaulted. Read the act here.

Section 228 of the Act also provides for compensation to victims of rape and other applicable offences. The provision requires the offender to pay emotional compensation to the victim.

In cases where the offender does not have sufficient property to provide compensation, the court can order an appropriate amount to be provided to the victim through the government body responsible for matters concerning women and children.

Thus, the provisions of the Criminal Code Act, 2074 clearly distinguish punishments based on the age and circumstances of the victim. Under Section 219(3), rape of a girl below 10 years of age can result in life imprisonment. Therefore, in the case of a three-year-old girl, the law provides for life imprisonment.

By contrast, Section 219(4) provides for imprisonment of up to five years for marital rape when a husband forces his wife to have sexual intercourse while the marital relationship continues.

Claim

The current law of Nepal has not been able to distinguish punishment by classifying it according to the type of rape. The rape of a three-year-old girl and marital rape are seen on the same scale. Therefore, to classify it, the law amendment process should be started immediately.

Claimant

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) MP Ashika Tamang.

Facts

Under Chapter 18 of the Criminal Code Act, 2074, Section 219 contains clear legal provisions prescribing different punishments for rape based on the age and circumstances of the victim.

Punishment for rape of girl child: According to sub-section (3)(a) of Section 219, rape of a girl below 10 years of age is punishable by life imprisonment.

Punishment for Marital Rape: According to sub-section (4) of Section 219, a husband who forces his wife to have sexual intercourse while the marital relationship continues can be sentenced to imprisonment for up to five years.

Classification according to age and condition: The law prescribes different punishments based on circumstances including the victim being below 10 years, 10 to 14 years, 14 to 16 years, 16 to 18 years, or 18 years or above. It also provides additional punishment in cases involving disabled or pregnant women, gang rape and other aggravated circumstances.

Conclusion

The claim that Nepal’s existing law places the rape of a three-year-old girl and marital rape on the same scale is false.

The Criminal Code Act, 2074 clearly provides different punishments depending on the nature and circumstances of the offence and the age and condition of the victim. While rape of a girl below 10 years of age can result in life imprisonment, marital rape is separately punishable by imprisonment of up to five years under Section 219(4).

Summoned by the Speaker, Nepal Prime Minister Balendra 'Balen' Shah will appear in Parliament on Wednesday (August 26). However, lawmakers who got the PM to attend the proceedings, won't be able to see eye to eye with him. The reason: Balen Shah will keep his dark sunglasses on even in Parliament.

Use of dark glasses was prohibited in Parliament by Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal but Balen Shah has found a way around.

Nepali media outlets reported on Tuesday that an ophthalmologist had suggested that Balen Shah wear dark sunglasses to protect his eye and use eyedrops.

Shah had gone for a check-up at the Birendra Military Hospital in Chhauni and was reviewed by Associate Professor Lieutenant Colonel Dr Sachit Dhakal, according to The Kathmandu Post.

Shah is scheduled to take direct questions from lawmakers and the report of the medical examination comes just a day ahead of that.

The dark glasses have been part of the persona of Balen Shah, a rapper-turned-politician, who is heading a majority government after years in Nepal. The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which fielded Shah, has a near two-thirds majority.

Shah was propelled to the PM's post after Gen Z protesters overthrew the KP Sharma Oli government in September 2025. While the youngsters see the dark glasses among Balen Shah's defiance, the Nepal PM's critics see it as a mark of his arrogance.

Shah has come in for criticism for his personality-based politics and undermining of democratic institutions and diplomatic norms. Even as he completed the first 150 days as PM, Shah seems to have lost much of his political shine.

Experts have slammed Shah for his confrontational attitude and concentrating power in his hands.

Balen Shah is "alienating constituencies that any government eventually needs: the media, the intelligentsia, the opposition parties and key foreign partners", wrote Biswas Baral, the former Editor of The Kathmandu Post, for The Diplomat in June.

In a recent column in The Kathmandu Times, analyst Samar SJB Rana asked whether Nepal, after overthrowing one political order, risks replacing it with something equally dependent on one personality. "Nepal wants no Caesar," he wrote.

The reference was to Julius Caesar, a symbol of absolute power and autocracy.

His refusal to take off the shades, despite providing a medical certificate, will be seen as another instance of his defiance.

Balen Shah, forced by Nepal's lawmakers, will be attending House proceedings but he will keep wearing his trademark sunglasses.
